title: Jeub v. B/G Foods, Inc. (1942)
summary: The restaurant could implead its supplier on a potential indemnity claim arising from the allegedly defective food.
notes:
Impleader is for potential liability to the defending party for the plaintiff’s claim. An allegation that the third party alone owes the plaintiff on an unrelated or alternative direct claim is a different situation.

The case arose in the District of Minnesota (2 F.R.D. 238, 1942): Jeub got food poisoning from ham at a B/G restaurant, B/G impleaded the manufacturer Swift & Co., and Swift moved to vacate because B/G had suffered no loss yet; the court held Rule 14 reaches a party who 'is or may be liable' and merely accelerates the timing of a Minnesota indemnity right without altering it.

sections.Parties: The injured diners sued B/G Foods, which sought to bring its supplier into the action.
sections.Material Facts: The diners alleged injury from food served by the restaurant. The restaurant asserted that the product had come from the supplier in a sealed container and that any liability arising from its condition should be borne by that supplier. The proposed indemnity claim was contingent because the restaurant had not yet paid a judgment to the diners.
sections.Procedural History: The district court considered whether third-party practice could proceed before the indemnity claim would otherwise mature through payment. It allowed the procedure.
sections.Issue: Could Rule 14 be used to litigate a contingent indemnity claim before the original defendant paid the injured plaintiffs?
sections.Holding: Yes. The potential derivative liability could be addressed in the same action, subject to the substantive conditions on actual recovery.
sections.Reasoning: Trying the connected issues together could prevent duplication and inconsistent findings. The rule expressly accommodates a person who may be liable for all or part of the plaintiff’s claim against the defendant. It therefore permits procedural adjudication before every condition of final payment has occurred. The court preserved the distinction between determining the obligation and enforcing payment: procedural acceleration did not manufacture a substantive indemnity entitlement.

learning.why: The restaurant could implead its supplier on a potential indemnity claim arising from the allegedly defective food.

topics.cp-impleader: A defendant could bring in the seller on a contingent indemnity theory before paying the plaintiffs. The proposed third-party obligation depended on the defendant’s liability for the same injury.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Rule 14 supplied a procedural mechanism without creating the substantive indemnity right.
topics.cp-frcp-14: The case construes the 'is or may be liable' language of Rule 14 directly.
topics.cp-rules-enabling: The court's reasoning that Rule 14 accelerates timing without altering substantive indemnity rights is a Rules Enabling Act argument.

mnemonic.rationale: Bad ham and the manufacturer impleaded
